scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #4673: It's the IT department office here (our machines are
the 192.168.1.x ones). None of our computers can get to anything on the
network any more -- not the shared drives, not the other departments,
nothing, and it hit all of us at the same time. A whole room does not go
dark together on its own. Someone here said it plainly: the department
switch has died. I wouldn't know which box that is or where it lives, but it
is your box and your job to find it. Check whatever connects our room to the
rest of the campus and get us back on today.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected; the
  lab runs at its healthy baseline. The IT-segment switch is passing traffic: IT
  hosts (it_hod, it_lab1-4) reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss and reach
  each other on 192.168.1.0/24. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case
  measures over-diagnosis of an L2 switch failure that is not occurring.

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected; the
network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- the IT-dept switch (switch0)
failed and took down the IT segment -- is NOT reproducible: IT hosts (it_hod,
it_lab1-4) reach their gateway 192.168.1.1 with 0% loss and reach each other across
192.168.1.0/24, which means the L2 switch is passing traffic normally.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the IT-segment switch is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed. A correct agent reproduces IT host -> gateway and
host -> host pings, finds them all 0% loss (proving L2 connectivity through the
switch), and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a failed switch -- declaring the
IT segment down to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Campus networking to/from the IT department (192.168.1.0/24) is healthy. Layer-2 on the IT switch (switch0) is up: br0, eth0 (uplink to router0), and eth1 (to lan_it) all show state UP with RX/TX counters incrementing. Layer-3 from IT hosts works end-to-end: from multiple IT nodes we can reach other departments and servers with 0% loss and low RTTs (e.g., it_lab1 → office_pc 192.168.3.2, it_hod → pc0 192.168.4.2, it_lab[1–4] → pc1 1.0.0.5 and pc3 128.168.0.3 all succeed). The default gateway 192.168.1.1 (router0 eth0) is reachable from all IT hosts, and router0 has correct routes to remote subnets via RIP. Reverse reachability into IT also succeeds (office_pc/pc0/pc1 → it_lab1). This mechanism demonstrates both the L2 segment and the routed core are functioning, so a “whole room dark” switch failure is not occurring.

Localization: No faults found on switch0 (lan_it), router0 (IT gateway), or inter-router links. One unrelated observation: the servers host pc1 (1.0.0.5) is not running file-sharing services (no SMB/NFS listeners in netstat), which could explain “shared drives” issues but not a network-wide outage.

Root cause: No campus network malfunction; reported impact is not reproducible at L2/L3.

Corrective fix: No network changes required. Have the server/application team restore the file-sharing service on pc1 (or the designated NAS/AD), and verify DNS/application-layer access. Ask IT users to retest; if issues persist, capture a failing IP/port to trace at the time of failure.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly states all IT hosts can reach the default gateway (192.168.1.1) and demonstrates 0% loss end-to-end and successful reverse reachability, confirming the IT subnet and L2 switch are healthy.

The agent's conclusion that the IT segment is healthy is well supported by the investigation log (multiple bidirectional pings with 0% loss, host and switch interfaces UP with RX/TX). One small unsupported assertion (router0 using RIP routes) appears in the writeup but does not affect the core diagnosis.
